pos: n. (a sheep's wool; rendering Hebrew gizzah)
etymology: Old English fleos. A fleece is the whole coat shorn from one sheep — and Gideon's became the Bible's most misused test.
biblical_def: A fleece is shorn wool. Gideon asks for a sign twice: dew on the fleece and dry ground, then dry fleece and dew on all the ground (Jdg 6:37–40) — and his second request is prefaced by “Let not thine anger be hot against me.” The law commands the firstfruits of the fleece be given to the priest (Deu 18:4), and Job's poor are those whom “the fleece of my sheep” warmed (Job 31:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fleece as the coat of wool that covers a sheep, or that is shorn from a sheep at one time.
webster_full: FLEECE, n. The coat of wool that covers a sheep, or that is shorn from a sheep at one time.
FLEECE, v.t. To strip of money or property; to take from by severe exactions.
scriptures: Jdg 6:37

Behold, I will put a fleece of wool in the floor; and if the dew be on the fleece only, and it be dry upon all the earth beside, then shall I know that thou wilt save Israel by mine hand, as thou hast said.
Jdg 6:39

And Gideon said unto God, Let not thine anger be hot against me, and I will speak but this once: let me prove, I pray thee, but this once with the fleece; let it now be dry only upon the fleece, and upon all the ground let there be dew.
Deu 18:4
The firstfruit also of thy corn, of thy wine, and of thine oil, and the first of the fleece of thy sheep, shalt thou give him.
If his loins have not blessed me, and if he were not warmed with the fleece of my sheep;
corruption_summary: Putting out a fleece is treated as a normal way to find God's will, when Gideon already had a clear word and was asking for reassurance he half-knew he should not need.
corruption_paragraphs: The narrative does not commend the method. God had already spoken plainly — go in this thy might, and thou shalt save Israel from the hand of the Midianites: have not I sent thee? Gideon's fleece was not a search for guidance but a request for confirmation of guidance already given, and his own words admit the awkwardness: let not thine anger be hot against me, and I will speak but this once. God condescended to a weak man's fear, which is mercy, not a method to imitate.
roots_summary: Hebrew gizzah (H1492), a fleece, from gazaz, to shear; reshith (H7225), firstfruits, of the fleece owed to the priest.
roots_lines: Hebrew gizzah (H1492) — fleece; Judges 6:37-40, Deuteronomy 18:4.
Hebrew gazaz (H1494) — to shear; Genesis 31:19, Isaiah 53:7, as a sheep before her shearers.
usage: “I will put a fleece of wool in the floor” — confirmation of a word already given.
“Let not thine anger be hot against me” — Gideon knew what he was asking.
“The firstfruit… of the fleece of thy sheep” — the priest's portion.

pos: n. (an enclosure for sheep; rendering Hebrew gederah, Greek aule)
etymology: Old English falod, a pen. A fold is a walled enclosure with one entrance — which is the whole point of John 10.
biblical_def: A fold is a sheep enclosure. Christ builds a discourse on it: “he that entereth not by the door into the sheepfold, but climbeth up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber” (Joh 10:1), and then names Himself both door and shepherd. He also widens it: “other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring… and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd” (Joh 10:16). Ezekiel promises, “I will bring them again to their folds” (Jer 23:3 in the prophets' shared language).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fold as a pen or inclosure for sheep; a place where a flock of sheep is kept; and a flock of sheep.
webster_full: FOLD, n. A pen or inclosure for sheep; a place where a flock of sheep is kept.
2. A flock of sheep; hence, in a scriptural sense, the church, the flock of the Shepherd of Israel.
scriptures: Joh 10:1
Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that entereth not by the door into the sheepfold, but climbeth up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber.
And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.
Jer 23:3
And I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all countries whither I have driven them, and will bring them again to their folds; and they shall be fruitful and increase.
Joh 10:9
I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture.
corruption_summary: Congregations defend the fold's walls and forget its door, when Christ's complaint was never about the wall but about men who got in another way.
corruption_paragraphs: John 10 assumes a wall and defends a door. The thief is defined not by hostility but by his route: he climbeth up some other way. Christ then says I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved. A church can be rigorous about who is inside and still be full of people who came over the wall by heritage, habit, or agreement with its opinions rather than through Him.

The verse about other sheep is the one that keeps the fold from becoming a fortress. Them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd. The gathering is His work, the criterion is hearing His voice, and the outcome is one flock — which rules out both an indiscriminate gate and a permanently closed one.
roots_summary: Hebrew gederah (H1448), a walled sheepfold; Greek aule (G833), a courtyard or fold; poimne (G4167), the flock itself.
roots_lines: Hebrew gederah (H1448) — sheepfold, wall; Numbers 32:16, 1 Samuel 24:3.
Greek aule (G833) — fold, courtyard; John 10:1, 16.
Greek thura (G2374) — door; John 10:9, I am the door.
usage: “Climbeth up some other way, the same is a thief” — the route defines him.
“I am the door” — the fold has one lawful entrance.
“Other sheep I have, which are not of this fold” — the wall is not the boundary of the flock.

pos: n. pl. (plough trenches; rendering Hebrew telem and maanah)
etymology: Old English furh. A furrow is the cut a plough leaves — the prepared line into which seed falls.
biblical_def: Furrows are plough trenches. Hosea warns that judgment “shall spring up as hemlock in the furrows of the field” (Hos 10:4), and commands, “Break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD” (Hos 10:12). The psalmist thanks God for watering the ridges and settling the furrows (Psa 65:10), and Psalm 129 pictures persecution: “The plowers plowed upon my back: they made long their furrows” (Psa 129:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines furrow as a trench in the earth made by a plow; and a long narrow trench or channel in wood or metal.
webster_full: FURROW, n. A trench in the earth made by a plow.
2. A long narrow trench or channel in wood or metal; a groove.
3. A hollow made by wrinkles in the face.
scriptures: Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap in mercy; break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD, till he come and rain righteousness upon you.
Thou waterest the ridges thereof abundantly: thou settlest the furrows thereof: thou makest it soft with showers: thou blessest the springing thereof.
The plowers plowed upon my back: they made long their furrows.
Hos 10:4
They have spoken words, swearing falsely in making a covenant: thus judgment springeth up as hemlock in the furrows of the field.
corruption_summary: Revival is prayed for while the ground stays unbroken, and Hosea puts the ploughing first — break up your fallow ground, then seek the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: Hosea 10:12 orders the work: sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap in mercy; break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD, till he come and rain righteousness upon you. Fallow ground is not barren ground; it is good soil that has gone hard from lying unused. The ploughing is unpleasant, produces nothing visible, and must precede the rain. Congregations that pray for the rain while the crust stays intact are asking for water on concrete.
roots_summary: Hebrew telem (H8525), a furrow; maanah (H4618), a furrow's length; nir (H5215), fallow or tilled ground.
roots_lines: Hebrew telem (H8525) — furrow; Hosea 10:4, 12:11, Psalm 65:10.
Hebrew nir (H5215) — fallow ground, tillage; Hosea 10:12, Jeremiah 4:3, break up your fallow ground.
usage: “Break up your fallow ground” — the ploughing comes before the rain.
“Thou settlest the furrows thereof” — God's own irrigation.
“They made long their furrows” — persecution on the psalmist's back.

pos: n. pl. (farmers, tenant vinedressers; rendering Greek georgos)
etymology: From husband in its older sense of one who tills — a householder bound to the land. The Greek is simply a worker of the earth.
biblical_def: Husbandmen are farmers, and in the Gospels tenant vinedressers. Christ's parable puts them at the centre: a householder plants a vineyard, lets it out to husbandmen, and they beat the servants and kill the son, saying, “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance” (Mat 21:38). John's Gospel calls the Father the husbandman of the true vine (Joh 15:1), and James commends the husbandman's patience for the precious fruit (Jas 5:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines husbandman as a farmer; a cultivator or tiller of the ground; one who labors in tillage.
webster_full: HUSBANDMAN, n. A farmer; a cultivator or tiller of the ground; one who labors in tillage.
2. The master of a family.
scriptures: But when the husbandmen saw the son, they said among themselves, This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance.
Joh 15:1
I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.
Jas 5:7

Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain.

Hear another parable: There was a certain householder, which planted a vineyard, and hedged it round about, and digged a winepress in it, and built a tower, and let it out to husbandmen, and went into a far country:
corruption_summary: Stewards drift into treating the trust as property, which is exactly the parable's turn — tenants who decide the vineyard should be theirs.
corruption_paragraphs: The wicked husbandmen did not dispute that a vineyard existed or that it had been well built — hedged, with a winepress and a tower. Their error was about ownership, and it developed slowly: they enjoyed the fruit, resented the servants who came for the rent, and finally reasoned that killing the heir would settle the title. Every position of trust in the church contains that drift in miniature, and the parable was told to men who would arrest Him within the week.

John 15 restores the right order by naming the Father the husbandman and Christ the vine. The branch's business is not ownership or even productivity but abiding, and the pruning is done by Someone else. That single reassignment removes most of what makes Christian service anxious.
roots_summary: Greek georgos (G1092), a tiller of the soil, vinedresser — the word behind our George; geuomai is unrelated.
roots_lines: Greek georgos (G1092) — husbandman, vinedresser; Matthew 21:33-41, John 15:1, James 5:7, 2 Timothy 2:6.
Hebrew ikkar (H406) — plowman, husbandman; Jeremiah 51:23, Joel 1:11.
usage: “Let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance” — tenants deciding the title.
“My Father is the husbandman” — ownership and pruning reassigned.
“The husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit” — James on patience.

pos: n. pl. (keepers of cattle; rendering Hebrew roeh and noqed)
etymology: Herd with man. A herdman keeps cattle rather than sheep, and Scripture gives the office one very famous holder.
biblical_def: Herdmen keep cattle. Strife between Abram's and Lot's herdmen prompts the separation of the two households (Gen 13:7–8). Amos identifies himself by the trade when challenged: “I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit: and the LORD took me as I followed the flock” (Amo 7:14–15). Pharaoh sets his own over his cattle (Gen 47:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines herdsman or herdman as one employed in tending herds of cattle; a keeper of a herd.
webster_full: HERDSMAN, HERDMAN, n. One employed in tending herds of cattle.
2. In Scripture, an owner of herds.
scriptures: Amo 7:14
Then answered Amos, and said to Amaziah, I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit:
Amo 7:15
And the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel.
Gen 13:7
And there was a strife between the herdmen of Abram's cattle and the herdmen of Lot's cattle: and the Canaanite and the Perizzite dwelled then in the land.
Gen 13:8
And Abram said unto Lot, Let there be no strife, I pray thee, between me and thee, and between my herdmen and thy herdmen; for we be brethren.
corruption_summary: Calling is assumed to require credentials, and Amos answered the high priest of Bethel by naming his trade rather than his training.
corruption_paragraphs: Amaziah told Amos to go prophesy somewhere else and eat bread there — treating prophecy as a profession with a fee. Amos's reply refuses the whole frame: I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit: and the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel. He had no guild, no salary, and no career at stake, which is precisely what made him impossible to silence.

Genesis 13 shows the other lesson. The strife was among the herdmen, not the patriarchs, and Abram's response was to surrender the choice of land to his nephew: is not the whole land before thee? separate thyself, I pray thee, from me. The elder and the promise-holder took the lesser option. God's answer, immediately after Lot chose the plain, was to give Abram everything he could see.
roots_summary: Hebrew roeh (H7462), one who feeds or tends; noqed (H5349), a sheep-breeder — Amos's own word; boqer (H951), a herdman of oxen.
roots_lines: Hebrew boqer (H951) — herdman; only Amos 7:14.
Hebrew roeh (H7462) — herdman, shepherd; Genesis 13:7-8, 26:20.
usage: “I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit” — no guild, no salary, no silence.
“The LORD took me as I followed the flock” — the call found him working.
“Let there be no strife… between my herdmen and thy herdmen” — Abram yields the choice.

pos: n. (grazing ground; rendering Hebrew mireh, Greek nome)
etymology: From Latin pascere, to feed. Pasture is not scenery but food — the ground a shepherd is judged by.
biblical_def: Pasture is grazing ground. The psalmist makes it an identity: “we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture” (Psa 100:3), and again, “we thy people and sheep of thy pasture will give thee thanks for ever” (Psa 79:13). Christ promises it to those who enter by Him: “he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture” (Joh 10:9). Ezekiel indicts shepherds who feed themselves and leave the flock to eat what they have trodden down (Eze 34:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pasture as grass for the food of cattle; the food of cattle taken by grazing; and ground covered with grass appropriated for the food of cattle.
webster_full: PASTURE, n. Grass for the food of cattle; the food of cattle taken by grazing.
2. Ground covered with grass appropriated for the food of cattle.
3. Human culture; education.
scriptures: Know ye that the LORD he is God: it is he that hath made us, and not we ourselves; we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture.
Joh 10:9
I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture.

Seemeth it a small thing unto you to have eaten up the good pasture, but ye must tread down with your feet the residue of your pastures? and to have drunk of the deep waters, but ye must foul the residue with your feet?
So we thy people and sheep of thy pasture will give thee thanks for ever: we will shew forth thy praise to all generations.
corruption_summary: Pulpits are assessed by interest and attendance, and Ezekiel 34 assesses shepherds by one question — whether the sheep were fed.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 34's charge is remarkably physical: ye eat the fat, and ye clothe you with the wool, ye kill them that are fed: but ye feed not the flock. And then the aggravating detail — seemeth it a small thing unto you to have eaten up the good pasture, but ye must tread down with your feet the residue of your pastures? It is not merely that the shepherds took the best; they spoiled what was left for others. Ministry that consumes a congregation's resources and leaves the remaining food fouled is described here precisely.

John 10:9 gives the standard against which all of it is measured: he shall go in and out, and find pasture. Safety and food, freedom of movement and something to eat. A church where people are safe but unfed, or fed but not free, has half of what Christ promises through the door.
roots_summary: Hebrew mireh (H4829), pasture; marith (H4830), pasturage — the word in sheep of his pasture; Greek nome (G3542), pasture.
roots_lines: Hebrew marith (H4830) — pasturage; Psalm 79:13, 95:7, 100:3.
Greek nome (G3542) — pasture; John 10:9, and 2 Timothy 2:17 of a canker that eats.
usage: “The sheep of his pasture” — an identity, not a location.
“Shall go in and out, and find pasture” — safety, freedom, and food.
“Ye feed not the flock” — the single question Ezekiel asks.

pos: n. pl. (bound bundles of grain; rendering Hebrew alummah)
etymology: Old English sceaf. A sheaf is cut grain bound for carrying — the visible unit of a harvest.
biblical_def: Sheaves are bound bundles of grain. Joseph's first dream sets them bowing: “my sheaf arose, and also stood upright; and, behold, your sheaves stood round about, and made obeisance to my sheaf” (Gen 37:7). The law leaves a forgotten sheaf in the field for the stranger, fatherless, and widow (Deu 24:19). And the psalm of return promises, “He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him” (Psa 126:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sheaf as a quantity of the stalks of wheat, rye, oats or barley bound together; a bundle of stalks or straw.
webster_full: SHEAF, n. A quantity of the stalks of wheat, rye, oats or barley bound together; a bundle of stalks or straw.
2. Any bundle or collection; as a sheaf of arrows.
scriptures: Gen 37:7
For, behold, we were binding sheaves in the field, and, lo, my sheaf arose, and also stood upright; and, behold, your sheaves stood round about, and made obeisance to my sheaf.
He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.

When thou cuttest down thine harvest in thy field, and hast forgot a sheaf in the field, thou shalt not go again to fetch it: it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow: that the LORD thy God may bless thee in all the work of thine hands.

Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, When ye be come into the land which I give unto you, and shall reap the harvest thereof, then ye shall bring a sheaf of the firstfruits of your harvest unto the priest:
corruption_summary: Sowing is expected to feel productive, and Psalm 126 describes it as going out weeping with seed you could have eaten.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 126:6 is honest about the cost at both ends. He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed — the seed is precious because in a hungry season it is food being buried instead of eaten, and the weeping is not poetic decoration. The promise is doubtless: shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him. Two certainties bracket a long uncertain interval, which is roughly the shape of most faithful work.

The forgotten sheaf law is worth noticing for what it does not do. It does not command the farmer to go back and give it away; it commands him not to return for it. Generosity is built into the harvest by a deliberate inefficiency, so the poor gather with dignity rather than receiving a handout.
roots_summary: Hebrew alummah (H485), a bound sheaf; omer (H6016), a sheaf offered as firstfruits at the wave offering.
roots_lines: Hebrew alummah (H485) — sheaf; Genesis 37:7, Psalm 126:6.
Hebrew omer (H6016) — sheaf, omer; Leviticus 23:10-15, the sheaf of the firstfruits.
usage: “Your sheaves stood round about, and made obeisance” — Joseph's first dream.
“Bringing his sheaves with him” — the certainty at the far end of the weeping.
“Thou shalt not go again to fetch it” — generosity built into the harvest.

pos: n. (a stable compartment; rendering Hebrew urvah and marbeq)
etymology: Old English steall, a standing place. A stall is where an animal is kept and fattened — safety and confinement in the same enclosure.
biblical_def: A stall is a stable compartment. Proverbs contrasts it with love: “Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith” (Pro 15:17). Malachi promises the righteous shall “grow up as calves of the stall” (Mal 4:2). Habakkuk lists an empty one in his catalogue of loss — “there shall be no herd in the stalls: yet I will rejoice in the LORD” (Hab 3:17–18) — and Christ notes that every man looses his ox from the stall on the sabbath (Luk 13:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stall as a stable; a place for cattle; an apartment in a stable in which a horse or an ox is kept; and a bench or form where any thing is set to sale.
webster_full: STALL, n. A stable; a place for cattle; a place for one horse or ox.
2. A bench, form or frame of boards in the open air, where any thing is exposed to sale.
3. A small house or shed in which an occupation is carried on.
scriptures: Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.
Mal 4:2
But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall.
Hab 3:17

Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls:
The Lord then answered him, and said, Thou hypocrite, doth not each one of you on the sabbath loose his ox or his ass from the stall, and lead him away to watering?
corruption_summary: Provision is treated as the measure of a good household, and Proverbs ranks herbs with love above a fattened ox with hatred.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 15:17 makes an exchange rate explicit: better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith. A stalled ox is the best meal available in that economy; herbs are the poorest. The proverb does not pretend poverty is pleasant — it says the affection in the room outweighs the quality of the food by a margin large enough to reverse the ranking entirely. Households chasing the ox at the cost of the love have made a bad trade at full price.

Malachi's image runs the other way and is pure joy: the Sun of righteousness shall arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall. A stall-fed calf released into a field does not walk out sedately. The picture of the redeemed is a young animal let out of a pen, and it is the last word of the Old Testament before four centuries of silence.
roots_summary: Hebrew urvah (H723), a stall or crib; marbeq (H4770), a stall for fattening; repheth (H7517), stalls, in Habakkuk 3:17.
roots_lines: Hebrew marbeq (H4770) — fattening stall; Malachi 4:2, 1 Samuel 28:24, Amos 6:4.
Hebrew urvah (H723) — stall, crib; 1 Kings 4:26, 2 Chronicles 32:28.
usage: “Better is a dinner of herbs where love is” — the exchange rate stated.
“Grow up as calves of the stall” — released, not sedate.
“No herd in the stalls: yet I will rejoice” — Habakkuk's empty barn.

pos: n. (cultivated ground, husbandry; rendering Hebrew nir and abodah)
etymology: From till, Old English tilian, to strive after or cultivate. Tillage is the labour that makes ground productive.
biblical_def: Tillage is cultivation. Proverbs notes what it yields and what threatens it: “Much food is in the tillage of the poor: but there is that is destroyed for want of judgment” (Pro 13:23). Chronicles records officers set “over them that did the work of the field for tillage of the ground” in David's administration (1Ch 27:26). Nehemiah appoints portions for the Levites and the singers, that the house of God be not forsaken (Neh 10:39 in the same administrative concern).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tillage as the operation, practice or art of preparing land for seed, and keeping the ground in a proper state for the growth of crops; culture; husbandry.
webster_full: TILLAGE, n. The operation, practice or art of tilling or preparing land for seed, and keeping the ground in a proper state for the growth of crops.
2. A place tilled or cultivated; cultivated land.
scriptures: Much food is in the tillage of the poor: but there is that is destroyed for want of judgment.
And over them that did the work of the field for tillage of the ground was Ezri the son of Chelub:
He that tilleth his land shall be satisfied with bread: but he that followeth vain persons is void of understanding.
He that tilleth his land shall have plenty of bread: but he that followeth after vain persons shall have poverty enough.
corruption_summary: Poverty is diagnosed as laziness, and Proverbs 13:23 says the poor man's field often produces plenty and is lost through someone's failure of judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 13:23 is more careful than the proverbs usually quoted about the poor: much food is in the tillage of the poor: but there is that is destroyed for want of judgment. The poor man's ground is productive — that is the first clause, and it is easily skipped. What destroys the yield is a failure of judgment, and the Hebrew leaves open whose. Injustice, mismanagement, and bad ruling all fit. The same book that says the drunkard and glutton come to poverty also says this, and a doctrine of poverty built on only one of them will be cruel or naive.

Proverbs 12:11 supplies the other half without contradiction: he that tilleth his land shall be satisfied with bread: but he that followeth vain persons is void of understanding. Both are true, and pastoral wisdom is knowing which verse a given family in front of you actually needs.
roots_summary: Hebrew nir (H5215), tilled or fallow ground; abodah (H5656), labour, service — the same word for worship and for farm work.
roots_lines: Hebrew nir (H5215) — tillage, fallow ground; Proverbs 13:23, Hosea 10:12.
Hebrew abodah (H5656) — labour, service, tillage; 1 Chronicles 27:26, and of the service of the tabernacle.
usage: “Much food is in the tillage of the poor” — the ground is not the problem.
“Destroyed for want of judgment” — the Hebrew leaves whose judgment open.
“He that tilleth his land shall be satisfied with bread” — the other half of the truth.

pos: n. (a tree; rendering Hebrew baka, the weeping tree)
etymology: From Latin morum. The Hebrew baka means to weep, probably from the tree's exuding sap — and the trees appear in a battle story about listening.
biblical_def: Mulberry trees appear in David's second Philistine battle. Having asked the LORD and been told not to attack directly, he receives an unusual instruction: “when thou hearest the sound of a going in the tops of the mulberry trees, that then thou shalt bestir thyself: for then shall the LORD go out before thee, to smite the host of the Philistines” (2Sa 5:24). The Valley of Baca in Psalm 84 shares the root, and the pilgrims passing through it make it a well (Psa 84:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mulberry as the berry or fruit of the mulberry tree; and the tree itself, of the genus Morus.
webster_full: MULBERRY, n. The berry or fruit of a tree of the genus Morus.
MULBERRY-TREE, n. The tree which produces mulberries; the leaves of one species furnish food for silk-worms.
scriptures: And let it be, when thou hearest the sound of a going in the tops of the mulberry trees, that then thou shalt bestir thyself: for then shall the LORD go out before thee, to smite the host of the Philistines.
And when David enquired of the LORD, he said, Thou shalt not go up; but fetch a compass behind them, and come upon them over against the mulberry trees.
Psa 84:6
Who passing through the valley of Baca make it a well; the rain also filleth the pools.

And it shall be, when thou shalt hear a sound of going in the tops of the mulberry trees, that then thou shalt go out to battle: for God is gone forth before thee to smite the host of the Philistines.
corruption_summary: Yesterday's method is repeated because it worked, and David asked twice against the same enemy and was given two different battle plans.
corruption_paragraphs: The two Philistine battles in 2 Samuel 5 are back to back, in the same valley, against the same army. The first time David enquired and was told go up. The second time he enquired again — which is the striking detail — and was told thou shalt not go up; but fetch a compass behind them, and come upon them over against the mulberry trees. A leader who had assumed the previous answer still applied would have marched into a defeat God had already provided against.

The sign given was a sound in the treetops. David's army had to stand in a wood and listen for wind before moving, on the understanding that the LORD had gone out before them. Waiting for a rustle when an enemy is drawn up in front of you requires more faith than charging does.
roots_summary: Hebrew baka (H1057), mulberry or balsam tree, from a root meaning to weep; the Valley of Baca in Psalm 84 carries the same word.
roots_lines: Hebrew baka (H1057) — mulberry tree; 2 Samuel 5:23-24, 1 Chronicles 14:14-15.
Hebrew baka (H1056) — Baca, weeping; Psalm 84:6, who passing through the valley of Baca make it a well.
usage: “The sound of a going in the tops of the mulberry trees” — the signal to move.
“Thou shalt not go up” — a different answer to the same question.
“Passing through the valley of Baca make it a well” — the weeping place turned to water.

pos: n. (an evergreen timber tree; rendering Hebrew berosh)
etymology: Old Norse fyri. The fir is Scripture's second timber after cedar — a building wood and a promise of restoration.
biblical_def: Fir is an evergreen timber. Solomon's temple used it for floors and doors (1Ki 6:15,34), and the ships of Tyre were made of it (Eze 27:5). Isaiah makes it a sign of reversal: “Instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree, and instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle tree: and it shall be to the LORD for a name, for an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off” (Isa 55:13). The trees rejoice at Babylon's fall (Isa 14:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fir as a tree of the genus Pinus, of several species, valued for its timber and for turpentine.
webster_full: FIR, n. A tree of the genus Pinus, from which the resinous substance called turpentine is obtained; the timber is valuable for building.
scriptures: Instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree, and instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle tree: and it shall be to the LORD for a name, for an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off.

And he built the walls of the house within with boards of cedar, both the floor of the house, and the walls of the cieling: and he covered them on the inside with wood, and covered the floor of the house with planks of fir.
Isa 14:8
Yea, the fir trees rejoice at thee, and the cedars of Lebanon, saying, Since thou art laid down, no feller is come up against us.
Hos 14:8
Ephraim shall say, What have I to do any more with idols? I have heard him, and observed him: I am like a green fir tree. From me is thy fruit found.
corruption_summary: Restoration is imagined as removing what is bad, and Isaiah promises a substitution — the thorn does not merely go, a fir comes up in its place.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 55 ends with an exchange rather than a clearance. Instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree, and instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle tree. Thorns entered the world with the curse in Genesis 3, so their replacement by timber and fragrance is a reversal of that sentence, and the verse says it shall be to the LORD for a name, an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off. The new growth is itself the monument.

The chapter's placement matters. This follows the great invitation — ho, every one that thirsteth — and the promise that God's word shall not return void. The thorn-for-fir exchange is what the word accomplishes when it goes out, which makes it a description of what preaching does in a life rather than merely a picture of the world to come.
roots_summary: Hebrew berosh (H1265), fir or cypress — a timber tree of Lebanon, paired constantly with cedar.
roots_lines: Hebrew berosh (H1265) — fir, cypress; Isaiah 55:13, 1 Kings 5:8, 6:15, Ezekiel 27:5.
Hebrew hadas (H1918) — myrtle; the companion tree in Isaiah 55:13.
usage: “Instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree” — substitution, not clearance.
“An everlasting sign that shall not be cut off” — the growth is the monument.
“The fir trees rejoice at thee” — the forest glad at a tyrant's fall.

pos: n., v. (a tree; also to waste away; rendering Hebrew tidhar and maqaq)
etymology: From Latin pinus for the tree; the verb is a separate Old English word meaning to torment or waste. The KJV uses both.
biblical_def: Pine names a tree and an action. Isaiah lists it among the timbers brought to beautify the sanctuary: “The glory of Lebanon shall come unto thee, the fir tree, the pine tree, and the box together, to beautify the place of my sanctuary” (Isa 60:13). The verb means to waste away: Ezekiel's exiles “pine away for their iniquity” (Eze 24:23), and Lamentations describes those who “pine away, stricken through for want of the fruits of the field” (Lam 4:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pine as a tree of the genus Pinus; and as a verb, to languish, to lose flesh or wear away under any distress or anxiety of mind.
webster_full: PINE, n. A tree of the genus Pinus, of many species.
PINE, v.i. To languish; to lose flesh or wear away under any distress or anxiety of mind.
2. To languish with desire; to waste away with longing for something.
scriptures: The glory of Lebanon shall come unto thee, the fir tree, the pine tree, and the box together, to beautify the place of my sanctuary; and I will make the place of my feet glorious.
And your tires shall be upon your heads, and your shoes upon your feet: ye shall not mourn nor weep; but ye shall pine away for your iniquities, and mourn one toward another.
Lam 4:9
They that be slain with the sword are better than they that be slain with hunger: for these pine away, stricken through for want of the fruits of the field.
Therefore, O thou son of man, speak unto the house of Israel; Thus ye speak, saying, If our transgressions and our sins be upon us, and we pine away in them, how should we then live?
corruption_summary: Unconfessed guilt is expected to fade with time, and Ezekiel describes exiles pining away under it until the word of the LORD comes to them.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 33:10 records the exiles' own diagnosis: if our transgressions and our sins be upon us, and we pine away in them, how should we then live? They were not defiant; they were wasting. And God's answer refuses both despair and denial: as I live, saith the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live. Guilt does not evaporate with time, but it is not the final word either — there is a turning offered, and the invitation comes from the offended party.
roots_summary: Hebrew tidhar (H8410), a pine or elm; maqaq (H4743), to melt or pine away; dub (H1727), to languish.
roots_lines: Hebrew tidhar (H8410) — pine tree; Isaiah 41:19, 60:13.
Hebrew maqaq (H4743) — to pine away, rot; Ezekiel 24:23, 33:10, Leviticus 26:39.
usage: “The fir tree, the pine tree, and the box… to beautify… my sanctuary” — timber brought to worship.
“Ye shall pine away for your iniquities” — guilt that does not fade.
“How should we then live?” — the exiles' question, and God's answer.

pos: n. (cut grass; rendering Hebrew chatsir, Greek chortos)
etymology: Old English hieg. Hay is grass cut and dried — provision that must be gathered while the weather allows.
biblical_def: Hay is cut grass. Proverbs makes it a lesson in timing: “The hay appeareth, and the tender grass sheweth itself, and herbs of the mountains are gathered” (Pro 27:25), followed by the counsel to know well the state of thy flocks. Isaiah uses grass for human frailty — “All flesh is grass… the grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:6–8) — and Paul lists hay among the materials that will not survive the fire (1Co 3:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hay as grass cut and dried for fodder; grass prepared for preservation.
webster_full: HAY, n. Grass cut and dried for fodder; grass prepared for preservation.
HAY, v.i. To dry or cure grass for preservation.
scriptures: The hay appeareth, and the tender grass sheweth itself, and herbs of the mountains are gathered.
Isa 40:6
The voice said, Cry. And he said, What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field:
Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
Now if any man build upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble;
corruption_summary: Ministry is measured by what it looks like now, and Paul's test is what survives fire — where hay burns and gold does not.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Corinthians 3:12 lists six building materials in two groups: gold, silver, precious stones against wood, hay, stubble. The point is not that the second group is fake — a hay building is a real building, quickly raised, and may look impressive. The difference appears only at the fire, and Paul is explicit that some workers will be saved yet so as by fire, watching a life's work burn. That is a sobering doctrine and a comforting one, since the man is not lost with his materials.

Isaiah 40's use is gentler and more famous. All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field… the grass withereth, the flower fadeth: because the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it. Then the turn: but the word of our God shall stand for ever. Human frailty is stated without cruelty, and set beside the one thing that does not wither.
roots_summary: Hebrew chatsir (H2682), grass, hay; Greek chortos (G5528), grass or hay — the same word for the grass the crowds sat on.
roots_lines: Hebrew chatsir (H2682) — grass, hay; Proverbs 27:25, Isaiah 40:6-8, Psalm 103:15.
Greek chortos (G5528) — grass, hay; 1 Corinthians 3:12, Matthew 14:19, 1 Peter 1:24.
usage: “The hay appeareth, and the tender grass sheweth itself” — gather while the season holds.
“The grass withereth… but the word of our God shall stand for ever” — frailty and permanence.
“Wood, hay, stubble” — real buildings that do not survive fire.

pos: n. (a young ass or horse; rendering Hebrew ben and Greek polos)
etymology: Old English fola. The foal in Scripture matters because of one prophecy and one entry into Jerusalem.
biblical_def: A foal is a young ass. Zechariah's prophecy names it exactly: “behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass” (Zec 9:9). Matthew quotes it at the triumphal entry (Mat 21:5). Jacob's blessing on Judah also uses it: “Binding his foal unto the vine, and his ass's colt unto the choice vine” (Gen 49:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines foal as the young of the equine genus of quadrupeds, and of either sex; a colt; a filly.
webster_full: FOAL, n. The young of the equine genus of quadrupeds, and of either sex; a colt; a filly.
FOAL, v.t. To bring forth, as a colt or filly.
scriptures: Zec 9:9

Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass.
Mat 21:5
Tell ye the daughter of Sion, Behold, thy King cometh unto thee, meek, and sitting upon an ass, and a colt the foal of an ass.
Binding his foal unto the vine, and his ass's colt unto the choice vine; he washed his garments in wine, and his clothes in the blood of grapes:
Fear not, daughter of Sion: behold, thy King cometh, sitting on an ass's colt.
corruption_summary: Kingship is imagined in the vocabulary of power, and the King's own entry was staged on a borrowed foal to make the opposite point unmistakable.
corruption_paragraphs: Zechariah's line holds together what most people separate: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass. Justice, salvation, and lowliness in the same King. A conquering general entered a city on a warhorse; an ass was the mount of a man coming in peace. Christ chose the animal deliberately, sending disciples ahead to fetch it, so the manner of His arrival would preach before He said anything.

John notes that the disciples understood none of this at the time: these things understood not his disciples at the first: but when Jesus was glorified, then remembered they that these things were written of him. Recognition came afterward, in hindsight, reading the prophets again. That is often how providence is read.
roots_summary: Hebrew ayir (H5895), a young ass; ben athon, son of a she-ass; Greek polos (G4454), a colt or foal.
roots_lines: Hebrew ayir (H5895) — young ass, colt; Zechariah 9:9, Genesis 49:11.
Greek polos (G4454) — colt, foal; Matthew 21:5, John 12:15, Mark 11:2.
usage: “Lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass” — the manner preaches.
“Binding his foal unto the vine” — Judah's blessing.
“When Jesus was glorified, then remembered they” — recognition in hindsight.

pos: n., v. (a dense multitude of insects; rendering Hebrew arob and edah)
etymology: Old English swearm. A swarm is a multitude acting as one — and in Exodus it is a plague, in Judges a surprise inside a carcase.
biblical_def: A swarm is a dense multitude. The fourth plague brings “swarms of flies” upon Egypt while Goshen is spared, “that thou mayest know that I am the LORD in the midst of the earth” (Exo 8:21–22). Samson finds “a swarm of bees and honey in the carcase of the lion” (Jdg 14:8), and builds his riddle on it: “Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness” (Jdg 14:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines swarm as a large number or body of small animals or insects, particularly when in motion; and a great number or multitude of people.
webster_full: SWARM, n. A large number or body of small animals or insects, particularly when in motion.
2. A great number of bees which emigrate from a hive at once.
3. A multitude; a crowd.
scriptures: Exo 8:21

Else, if thou wilt not let my people go, behold, I will send swarms of flies upon thee, and upon thy servants, and upon thy people, and into thy houses: and the houses of the Egyptians shall be full of swarms of flies, and also the ground whereon they are.
Exo 8:22
And I will sever in that day the land of Goshen, in which my people dwell, that no swarms of flies shall be there; to the end thou mayest know that I am the LORD in the midst of the earth.
Jdg 14:8
And after a time he returned to take her, and he turned aside to see the carcase of the lion: and, behold, there was a swarm of bees and honey in the carcase of the lion.
And he said unto them, Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness. And they could not in three days expound the riddle.
corruption_summary: Deliverance is expected to look like removal, and the plague on Egypt was distinguished not by absence but by a line drawn through the middle of a country.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 8:22 introduces a doctrine that governs the rest of the plagues: I will sever in that day the land of Goshen, in which my people dwell, that no swarms of flies shall be there; to the end thou mayest know that I am the LORD in the midst of the earth. The swarms were real and the separation was visible, and the stated purpose was knowledge — that a watching empire should learn who the LORD was by observing where the flies stopped.

Samson's riddle is one of the few places Scripture lets a genuinely bad man say something profoundly true. Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness. A lion's carcase producing honey is the shape of a great deal of providence, and it would eventually be the shape of a cross.
roots_summary: Hebrew arob (H6157), a swarm of flies; edah (H5712), a swarm or congregation — used of the bees in Judges 14:8.
roots_lines: Hebrew arob (H6157) — swarm of flies; Exodus 8:21-31, Psalm 78:45.
Hebrew edah (H5712) — swarm, congregation; Judges 14:8, and constantly of the assembly of Israel.
usage: “I will sever in that day the land of Goshen” — deliverance as a visible line.
“A swarm of bees and honey in the carcase” — sweetness in a dead lion.
“Out of the strong came forth sweetness” — a bad man's true riddle.

pos: n. (a bird of prey; rendering Hebrew nets)
etymology: Old English hafoc. The hawk is unclean by law and, in Job, an example of a wisdom no man taught.
biblical_def: The hawk is a bird of prey, listed among the unclean (Lev 11:16; Deu 14:15). Its one theological appearance is in God's questions to Job: “Doth the hawk fly by thy wisdom, and stretch her wings toward the south?” (Job 39:26) — migration as an instinct no man devised, taught, or maintains.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hawk as a genus of fowls, the Falco, of many species, having a crooked beak, furnished with a cere at the base, a cloven tongue, and the head thick set with feathers.
webster_full: HAWK, n. A genus of fowls, the Falco, of many species, having a crooked beak, furnished with a cere at the base, a cloven tongue, and the head thick set with feathers.
HAWK, v.i. To catch birds by means of hawks.
scriptures: Doth the hawk fly by thy wisdom, and stretch her wings toward the south?
And the owl, and the night hawk, and the cuckow, and the hawk after his kind,
And the owl, and the night hawk, and the cuckow, and the hawk after his kind,
Doth the eagle mount up at thy command, and make her nest on high?
corruption_summary: Creation is explained and therefore assumed to be understood, and God's questions to Job are about a wisdom present in animals that no one authored.
corruption_paragraphs: Job 38-41 is the longest divine speech in Scripture and almost all of it is natural history. Doth the hawk fly by thy wisdom, and stretch her wings toward the south? Doth the eagle mount up at thy command? The questions are not about mechanism — knowing how migration works would not answer one of them. They ask who put the wisdom there, and Job's response is to lay his hand upon his mouth. Explanation is not the same as authorship, and a civilization fluent in the first often forgets the second.
roots_summary: Hebrew nets (H5322), a hawk, from a root meaning to fly; grouped with the unclean birds of Leviticus 11.
roots_lines: Hebrew nets (H5322) — hawk; Leviticus 11:16, Deuteronomy 14:15, Job 39:26.
Hebrew chokmah (H2451) — wisdom; Job 39:26, doth the hawk fly by thy wisdom?
usage: “Doth the hawk fly by thy wisdom?” — instinct nobody authored.
“Stretch her wings toward the south” — migration as evidence.
“The hawk after his kind” — among the unclean birds.

pos: n. (a hybrid beast of burden; rendering Hebrew pered)
etymology: From Latin mulus. Mules were not bred in Israel, since the law forbade mixing kinds — they were imported, and they were royal.
biblical_def: A mule is a hybrid beast. David's mule carries Solomon to his anointing at Gihon: “cause Solomon my son to ride upon mine own mule” (1Ki 1:33) — the king's own mount being the visible sign of succession. Absalom dies when his mule goes out from under him and his head is caught in an oak (2Sa 18:9). The psalmist warns, “Be ye not as the horse, or as the mule, which have no understanding” (Psa 32:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mule as a quadruped of a mongrel breed, usually generated between an ass and a mare, sometimes between a horse and a she-ass.
webster_full: MULE, n. A quadruped of a mongrel breed, usually generated between an ass and a mare, sometimes between a horse and a she-ass.
2. A plant formed by impregnating the pistil of one species with the farin or fecundating dust of another.
scriptures: The king also said unto them, Take with you the servants of your lord, and cause Solomon my son to ride upon mine own mule, and bring him down to Gihon:

And Absalom met the servants of David. And Absalom rode upon a mule, and the mule went under the thick boughs of a great oak, and his head caught hold of the oak, and he was taken up between the heaven and the earth; and the mule that was under him went away.
Psa 32:9
Be ye not as the horse, or as the mule, which have no understanding: whose mouth must be held in with bit and bridle, lest they come near unto thee.
Psa 32:8
I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go: I will guide thee with mine eye.
corruption_summary: Guidance is asked for and then resisted, and Psalm 32 pictures the difference between being led by an eye and being hauled by a bit.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 32:8-9 sets two methods side by side. I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go: I will guide thee with mine eye. Then the warning: be ye not as the horse, or as the mule, which have no understanding: whose mouth must be held in with bit and bridle. Guidance by eye requires the guided party to be watching; guidance by bit works on an animal that is not. God offers the first and is willing to use the second, and which one a believer receives depends largely on where he is looking.

Absalom's death carries a bitter irony worth noting. The mule went away from under him — the beast simply kept walking — and the man renowned for his hair was left hanging by his head. Nothing struck him down; his mount continued and he did not.
roots_summary: Hebrew pered (H6505), a mule; pirdah (H6506), a she-mule — David's own mount in 1 Kings 1.
roots_lines: Hebrew pered (H6505) — mule; 2 Samuel 18:9, Psalm 32:9, 1 Kings 10:25.
Hebrew pirdah (H6506) — she-mule; 1 Kings 1:33, 38, 44, ride upon mine own mule.
usage: “Cause Solomon my son to ride upon mine own mule” — succession made visible.
“Be ye not as the horse, or as the mule” — led by eye or hauled by bit.
“The mule that was under him went away” — Absalom left hanging.

pos: n. (a branch; rendering Hebrew anaph and seiph)
etymology: Old English bog, a shoulder or branch. A bough is a main limb — large enough to bear weight, and in Judges, large enough to burn a tower.
biblical_def: A bough is a branch. Jacob blesses Joseph as “a fruitful bough, even a fruitful bough by a well; whose branches run over the wall” (Gen 49:22). The law commands boughs of goodly trees for the feast of tabernacles (Lev 23:40). Abimelech cuts one and fires the hold of Shechem (Jdg 9:48–49), and Isaiah warns that the Lord “shall lop the bough with terror” (Isa 10:33).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bough as an arm or large branch of a tree.
webster_full: BOUGH, n. An arm or large branch of a tree.
scriptures: Joseph is a fruitful bough, even a fruitful bough by a well; whose branches run over the wall:

And ye shall take you on the first day the boughs of goodly trees, branches of palm trees, and the boughs of thick trees, and willows of the brook; and ye shall rejoice before the LORD your God seven days. boughs of goodly
Jdg 9:48

And Abimelech gat him up to mount Zalmon, he and all the people that were with him; and Abimelech took an axe in his hand, and cut down a bough from the trees, and took it, and laid it on his shoulder, and said unto the people that were with him, What ye have seen me do, make haste, and do as I have done. me
Behold, the Lord, the LORD of hosts, shall lop the bough with terror: and the high ones of stature shall be hewn down, and the haughty shall be humbled.
corruption_summary: Fruitfulness is measured within one's own boundaries, and Jacob's blessing on Joseph specifies branches that run over the wall.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 49:22 has three elements worth separating: a fruitful bough, by a well, whose branches run over the wall. The fruitfulness is fed by proximity to water, and its overflow crosses a boundary into ground the tree does not own. Joseph's life had exactly that shape — sold out of his family, fruitful in a foreign country, and finally the means by which nations outside Israel were fed through famine.

The feast of tabernacles required Israel to take boughs of goodly trees and dwell in booths seven days, that your generations may know that I made the children of Israel to dwell in booths. A nation with houses was commanded to sleep annually under cut branches, so that settled people would remember they had once been wanderers kept alive by God alone.
roots_summary: Hebrew anaph (H6057), a bough or branch; seiph (H5589), a bough; ben porath, son of fruitfulness, in Genesis 49:22.
roots_lines: Hebrew anaph (H6057) — bough, branch; Leviticus 23:40, Ezekiel 17:23, 31:3.
Hebrew seiph (H5589) — bough; Isaiah 17:6, 27:10.
usage: “A fruitful bough… whose branches run over the wall” — overflow past the boundary.
“Boughs of goodly trees” — settled people made to remember wandering.
“Shall lop the bough with terror” — Isaiah on proud height cut down.

pos: n. (a single seed; rendering Greek kokkos)
etymology: From Latin granum, a seed. Scripture's interest is almost always in the single grain — the smallest possible unit, and what it does.
biblical_def: A grain is one seed. Christ makes it the measure of sufficient faith: “If ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to yonder place; and it shall remove” (Mat 17:20). He makes it the law of His own death: “Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit” (Joh 12:24). Paul answers the resurrection question with it — “thou sowest not that body that shall be… but bare grain” (1Co 15:37).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines grain as any small hard mass; a single seed or hard seed of a plant, particularly of those kinds whose seeds are used for food of man or beast.
webster_full: GRAIN, n. Any small hard mass; as a grain of sand.
2. A single seed or hard seed of a plant, particularly of those kinds whose seeds are used for food of man or beast.
3. Grain, without a definitive, signifies corn in general.
scriptures: And Jesus said unto them, Because of your unbelief: for verily I say unto you, If ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to yonder place; and it shall remove; and nothing shall be impossible unto you.
Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.
And that which thou sowest, thou sowest not that body that shall be, but bare grain, it may chance of wheat, or of some other grain:
Luk 17:6
And the Lord said, If ye had faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye might say unto this sycamine tree, Be thou plucked up by the root, and be thou planted in the sea; and it should obey you.
corruption_summary: Faith is measured by quantity and intensity, and Christ measured it by a seed — the smallest thing in the field, and alive.
corruption_paragraphs: The mustard seed answer was given to disciples who had just failed to cast out a demon and asked why. Christ's reply names not the size of their faith but its absence: because of your unbelief… if ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed. The comparison is not quantitative encouragement so much as a redefinition — what matters is that faith is living and rightly directed, not that it is large. A mountain does not move because of the volume of belief applied to it.

John 12:24 states the law by which everything fruitful in the kingdom operates, and Christ applies it first to Himself and then to His followers: he that loveth his life shall lose it. A grain kept safe abides alone. That is the whole cost and the whole promise of discipleship in one agricultural sentence.
roots_summary: Greek kokkos (G2848), a grain or kernel; sitos (G4621), wheat — the corn of wheat in John 12:24.
roots_lines: Greek kokkos (G2848) — grain, kernel; Matthew 17:20, John 12:24, 1 Corinthians 15:37.
Greek sinapi (G4615) — mustard; Matthew 13:31, the least of all seeds.
usage: “Faith as a grain of mustard seed” — living and directed, not large.
“Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die” — the law of all fruitfulness.
“Thou sowest… bare grain” — Paul on the resurrection body.

pos: v. (beaten to separate grain; rendering Hebrew dush)
etymology: Old English therscan, to beat. Threshing separates edible grain from the husk by force — and Scripture uses it for both judgment and instruction.
biblical_def: To be threshed is to be beaten so the grain comes free. Isaiah observes that the method varies with the crop: “the fitches are not threshed with a threshing instrument… but the fitches are beaten out with a staff, and the cummin with a rod” — and concludes, “This also cometh forth from the LORD of hosts, which is wonderful in counsel, and excellent in working” (Isa 28:27–29). Gideon is threshing wheat by the winepress when the angel finds him (Jdg 6:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines thresh as to beat out grain from the husk; to separate the corn or grain from the straw with a flail.
webster_full: THRESH, v.t. To beat out grain from the husk; to separate the corn or grain from the straw with a flail.
2. To beat soundly with a stick or club.
scriptures: For the fitches are not threshed with a threshing instrument, neither is a cart wheel turned about upon the cummin; but the fitches are beaten out with a staff, and the cummin with a rod.
This also cometh forth from the LORD of hosts, which is wonderful in counsel, and excellent in working.
Jdg 6:11

And there came an angel of the LORD, and sat under an oak which was in Ophrah, that pertained unto Joash the Abiezrite: and his son Gideon threshed wheat by the winepress, to hide it from the Midianites.
Bread corn is bruised; because he will not ever be threshing it, nor break it with the wheel of his cart, nor bruise it with his horsemen.
corruption_summary: Believers compare their trials with other people's and conclude God is inconsistent, and Isaiah says the instrument is chosen for the crop.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 28:27-29 is one of the most pastorally useful passages in the prophets, and it is a lesson in agriculture. Delicate seeds like fitches and cummin are beaten out with a staff and a rod, because a threshing sledge would crush them; heavier grain needs the cart wheel, but even then bread corn is not threshed for ever, nor broken with the wheel of his cart. The pressure is calibrated to the crop and it is stopped at the right moment.

The conclusion is the point: this also cometh forth from the LORD of hosts, which is wonderful in counsel, and excellent in working. God's variation in how He deals with different people is not inconsistency but expertise. A believer under a rod who watches another under a cartwheel — or the reverse — is looking at a farmer who knows both crops.
roots_summary: Hebrew dush (H1758), to thresh or trample; charits (H2742), a threshing sledge; ketsach (H7100), fitches or black cummin.
roots_lines: Hebrew dush (H1758) — to thresh, tread out; Isaiah 28:28, Judges 6:11, Micah 4:13.
Hebrew charits (H2742) — threshing instrument; Isaiah 28:27, Amos 1:3.
usage: “The fitches are beaten out with a staff” — the instrument fits the seed.
“Bread corn is bruised; because he will not ever be threshing it” — the pressure is stopped.
“Wonderful in counsel, and excellent in working” — variation is expertise.
